evidence.supportingExcerpt: An observational study records or reconstructs exposures without assigning them. A cohort follows a defined group over time; a case-control design selects people with and without an outcome and examines earlier exposures; a cross-sectional design measures a population at a time point. Prospective means forward follow-up, not randomized assignment. Such data can describe uncommon harms, care patterns and underrepresented populations. A causal claim about changing treatment requires more than an association. Random assignment reduces treatment-selection bias but cannot guarantee complete follow-up or applicability. In a fictional database, following treated and untreated groups forward from different dates does not randomize them.

canonicalTeaching.requirement: Randomization protects a within-trial contrast, not experimental-arm comparisons across separately conducted randomized trials.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A higher percentage in one paper is a reason to examine its study, rather than proof that its treatment is better. Randomisation protects comparisons within a trial, not between separately conducted trials. Comparing their experimental arms discards that protection. Disease burden, biomarker assay and threshold, prior treatment, background care, dose, endpoint rules, analysis population and follow-up can differ. Formal indirect comparison through a common comparator preserves each trial's treatment-versus-control contrast but still requires compatible questions and methods. Pooling active arms across trials is prone to bias, and even an adjusted indirect estimate remains less secure than a suitable direct comparison (Bucher and colleagues, 1997). Network meta-analysis adds a transitivity assumption: important effect modifiers must be sufficiently comparable across the network. A shared drug name or statistical agreement cannot establish that unmeasured compatibility. Similar endpoint labels can hide different definitions: a clinical benefit rate may include different durations of stable disease.
